chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Yunus, from Abu Al-Rabie Al-Shamy, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said:

He said to me: 'Woe be unto you, O Abu Al-Rabie! Do not seek the leadership, nor become a wolf, nor devour the people by us, so Allah would impoverish you. And do not say regarding us what we do not say regarding ourselves, for you will be made to pause and inevitably be questioned. So if you are truthful, we will ratify you, and if you are a liar, we will belie you.'

key_terms.الرِّئَاسَةَ: Leadership or headship, often referring to political or administrative authority
key_terms.تَأْكُلْ بِنَا النَّاسَ: To devour the people by us, meaning to exploit the community using the Imams' name or authority
key_terms.ذِئْباً: Wolf, used metaphorically for a predatory person who consumes others' rights or wealth
key_terms.مَسْئُولٌ: Questioned, regarding accountability for one's claims and actions
key_terms.مَوْقُوفٌ: Made to stand/pause, referring to being stopped for questioning on the Day of Judgment

ai.seo_question: What is the significance of seeking leadership (al-ri'asah) in Shia hadith and how do the Imams verify their narrators?
ai.summary: In this hadith from al-Kafi, Imam al-Baqir (AS) warns Abu Al-Rabie against seeking leadership (al-ri'asah) and acting as a 'wolf' that consumes the community's resources, a metaphor for exploitation. He establishes a criterion of authenticity by promising to verify his claims if true and refute them if false, highlighting the Imam's role as the ultimate arbiter of truth. This emphasizes the accountability of those who claim authority or knowledge, ensuring they do not mislead the faithful for personal gain.
